ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertain Correlation Regularization (UCR)
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel regularization term for policy optimization that upper-bounds the true reward under the assumption of uncertain correlation between the proxy reward and the true reward. Specifically, we use a robustified chi-squared divergence, which is sensitive to large deviations from the assumed correlation, to regularize the policy against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint. This allows us to derive a policy update rule that is computationally tractable and can be incorporated into standard policy-optimization methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization (e.g. PPO, SAC) without regularization; ablation: regularizing only against a single trusted proxy reward.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust guarantee against reward hacking than existing methods, but may come at the cost of a reduced policy performance due to added regularization; potential failure points are the choice of robustification strength and the assumption of uncertain correlation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Correlation Uncertainty with Empirical Distributions
PROPOSAL: To better quantify the uncertainty in the correlation between the proxy reward and the true reward, we propose an empirical distribution-based approach to estimate the distribution of true rewards given a proxy reward. We use a small exploratory dataset to generate a set of proxy-reward pairs and their corresponding true rewards, from which we estimate the distribution of true rewards. We then use this distribution to quantify the uncertainty in the correlation coefficient and select an optimal robustification strength for the UCR regularization term.
CONTROLS: Baseline: UCR with a fixed, arbitrary robustification strength; ablation: using a single estimated correlation coefficient instead of an empirical distribution.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the robustness of UCR by adapting to the true correlation distribution, but may require careful tuning of the exploratory dataset size and robustification strength; potential failure points include overfitting to the exploratory dataset and poorly estimated distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpretable Policy Regularization via Reference-Induced Occupancy Constraints
PROPOSAL: To improve the interpretability of policies learned using UCR, we propose using reference-induced occupancy constraints to regularize the learned policy against the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. This allows us to derive a policy that not only optimizes the proxy reward but also aligns with the reference policy's structure, providing insights into the decision-making process.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard UCR regularization without reference-induced constraints; ablation: using only reference-induced constraints without UCR regularization.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the interpretability of UCR-regularized policies and align them with expert knowledge, but may come at the cost of reduced policy performance; potential failure points include mismatch between the reference policy and the true reward or payout mapping.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Insulin Dosing for Type 1 Diabetes using UCR with Prior Knowledge
PROPOSAL: We apply UCR to the real-world problem of blood glucose control for patients with type 1 diabetes, incorporating prior knowledge about the true reward (e.g., glucose levels, medication side effects) into the regularization term. We use a synthetic dataset to simulate patient responses to different insulin dosing schedules and a real-world dataset of glucose sensor readings to validate our approach.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR without prior knowledge incorporation.
COST: 300 GPU-hours + 100 hours of real-world data processing
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and interpretable policy for insulin dosing, but may require careful selection of prior knowledge and tuning of the regularization strength; potential failure points include overfitting to the prior knowledge and mismatch between synthetic and real-world data.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Robust Autonomy for Highway Merging
PROPOSAL: We modify the Robust Insulin Dosing for Type 1 Diabetes experiment to instead apply UCR to the autonomous vehicle traffic control problem, specifically the task of highway merging. We simulate vehicle behavior using the SUMO simulator and design a scenario where a vehicle must merge into a high-speed traffic lane while avoiding collisions and optimizing its own motion. We use UCR with prior knowledge about safe merging distances and vehicle speeds.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR without prior knowledge incorporation.
COST: 300 GPU-hours + 100 hours of simulation data processing
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and interpretable policy for highway merging, but may require careful selection of prior knowledge and tuning of the regularization strength; potential failure points include overfitting to the prior knowledge and limited generalizability to real-world traffic scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Robust Autonomy for Highway Merging
PROPOSAL: REVISED: We apply UCR to the autonomous vehicle traffic control problem, specifically the task of highway merging. We simulate vehicle behavior using the SUMO simulator and design a scenario where a vehicle must merge into a high-speed traffic lane while avoiding collisions and optimizing its own motion. We use UCR with prior knowledge about safe merging distances and vehicle speeds, and evaluate the performance of UCR using different expert policies (e.g., TD3, SAC) as reference policies.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR without prior knowledge incorporation or reference- induced constraints.
COST: 300 GPU-hours + 100 hours of simulation data processing
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and interpretable policy for highway merging, but may require careful selection of prior knowledge and tuning of the regularization strength; potential failure points include overfitting to the prior knowledge and limited generalizability to real-world traffic scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Lockdown Policy Selection using UCR with Multi-Scenario Training
PROPOSAL: We propose using UCR to develop a robust lockdown policy for pandemic response by training the policy in different scenarios (e.g., low, medium, high transmission rates) while regularizing against the correlation between a proxy reward (e.g., social distancing adherence) and a true reward (e.g., reduced transmission rates). This approach allows the policy to adapt to the uncertainty in the true reward and perform well across different scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR without multi-scenario training.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and adaptive policy for lockdown response, but may require careful selection of scenario mix and training parameters; potential failure points include overfitting to specific scenarios and limited generalizability to real-world pandemic dynamics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving UCR with a Part-Whole Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating a part-whole attention mechanism into UCR to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of the state and action spaces when calculating the correlation between the proxy and true rewards. This should help UCR to better capture the complex relationships between the proxy and true rewards, leading to improved performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard UCR without attention mechanism; ablation: UCR with a simple attention mechanism (e.g., additive attention).
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the performance and robustness of UCR, but may require careful tuning of the attention mechanism parameters; potential failure points include overfitting to the attention mechanism and increased computational complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of UCR under Misspecified Correlation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the performance of UCR under misspecified correlation between the proxy and true rewards, where the true correlation is different from the assumed correlation. We design experiments to evaluate how well UCR can recover good policies under misspecification and explore the limits of its robustness.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR with a varying degree of misspecification.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide insights into the limits of UCR's robustness under misspecification and help identify opportunities for improvement, but may require careful design of experiments and analysis methods; potential failure points include overfitting to specific misspecification scenarios and difficulty in evaluating robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: UCR-based LLM Alignment via Reward Shaping
PROPOSAL: We apply UCR to the task of large language model (LLM) alignment via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where the goal is to shape the reward function to maximize user satisfaction. We use UCR to regularize the reward function against the correlation between proxy rewards (e.g., user feedback) and a true reward (e.g., user engagement). This approach allows us to develop more robust and interpretable reward functions that are aligned with human preferences.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard policy-optimization without regularization; ablation: UCR without reward shaping.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust and interpretable reward function for LLM alignment, but may require careful selection of proxy rewards and tuning of UCR parameters; potential failure points include overfitting to specific user preferences and difficulty in evaluating user engagement.

TITLE: Analyzing the Representation Power of Meta-Learned Random Features
PROPOSAL: Investigate the representation power of the meta-learned random feature design by analyzing its embedding capacity, linearity, and expressiveness on both stationary and non-stationary data using various tools such as PCA, t-SNE, and NN-based visualizations.
CONTROLS: Compare the representation power of the meta-learned random feature design with that of stationary random Fourier features, as well as a GP model with an expressive, non-stationary kernel (e.g., deep GP), on both speech signal analysis (LibriSpeech and speaker diarization datasets) and biological protein data regression (Prosite database and PBM dataset) benchmarks.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learned random feature design should exhibit improved representation power compared to stationary random Fourier features, particularly on non-stationary data, while maintaining competitiveness with the GP model on both stationary and non-stationary data.

This analysis will help us understand the capacity of the meta-learned random feature design to capture complex patterns in the data, and how it compares to other state-of-the-art methods. By visualizing the embedding spaces of different methods, we can gain insights into the representational power of each approach.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing the Representation Power of Meta-Learned Random Features: A Detailed Study
PROPOSAL: Perform a more in-depth analysis of the representation power of the meta-learned random feature design by evaluating its ability to capture non-linear relationships, handle outliers, and generalize across different data distributions and tasks using techniques such as permutation tests, sensitivity analysis, and ablation studies.
CONTROLS: Compare the representation power of the meta-learned random feature design with that of stationary random Fourier features, as well as a GP model with an expressive, non-stationary kernel (e.g., deep GP), on both speech signal analysis (LibriSpeech and speaker diarization datasets) and biological protein data regression (Prosite database and PBM dataset) benchmarks.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (incremental cost of adding more analysis techniques)
PREDICTION: The meta-learned random feature design should exhibit improved robustness and generalizability, handling outliers and non-linear relationships more effectively, and demonstrating competitiveness with the GP model on both stationary and non-stationary data.

This in-depth analysis will provide a better understanding of the strengths and limitations of the meta-learned random feature design, and help identify areas for further improvement. By evaluating its performance under various scenarios and using a range of analysis techniques, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of its representational power.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Introducing Attention-Based Meta-Learned Random Features
PROPOSAL: Modify the meta-learned random feature design to incorporate attention mechanisms, allowing the model to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of the input data while computing the features, and adaptively adjust the feature extraction mechanism based on the data distribution and task.
CONTROLS: Compare the attention-based meta-learned random feature design with the original meta-learned random feature design, as well as a GP model with an expressive, non-stationary kernel (e.g., deep GP), on both speech signal analysis (LibriSpeech and speaker diarization datasets) and biological protein data regression (Prosite database and PBM dataset) benchmarks.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The attention-based meta-learned random feature design should exhibit improved performance, particularly in scenarios where there are varying levels of complexity and relevance in the input data, and adapt more effectively to non-stationary data distributions, but may require careful tuning of the attention mechanisms to balance focus and exploration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Parallelization of Meta-Learned Random Features
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability and parallelization of the meta-learned random feature design, specifically the attention-based variant, using distributed computing architectures and techniques such as data parallelism, model parallelism, and gradient checkpointing, to enable efficient training and inference on large-scale datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the scalability and parallelization of the meta-learned random feature design with traditional GP models and other state-of-the-art methods, on large-scale speech signal analysis (e.g., LibriSpeech 960h) and biological protein data regression benchmarks.
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learned random feature design, particularly the attention-based variant, should demonstrate improved scalability and parallelization capabilities, enabling efficient training and inference on large-scale datasets, but may require careful optimization and tuning to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Meta-Learned Random Features to Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of the meta-learned random feature design, including the attention-based variant, to distribution shifts, such as adversarial attacks, corruptions, and out-of-distribution data, using techniques such as robustness benchmarking and transfer learning.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of the meta-learned random feature design with traditional GP models and other state-of-the-art methods, on various benchmarks, including speech signal analysis (e.g., LibriSpeech 960h) and biological protein data regression (e.g., Prosite database).
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learned random feature design, particularly the attention-based variant, should exhibit improved robustness to distribution shifts, but may require careful tuning of the attention mechanisms and feature extraction mechanism to balance robustness and performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Unified Framework for Random Feature Designs
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that integrates the various random feature designs proposed in this research, including perpetual templates, meta-learned features, and attention-based features, into a single, modular, and highly extensible architecture, allowing for easy comparison and combination of different design choices.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the unified framework on various benchmarks, including speech signal analysis and biological protein data regression, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 360 GPU-hours (incremental cost of integrating and testing the unified framework)
PREDICTION: The unified framework should provide a flexible and efficient way to design and evaluate random feature methods, enabling researchers and practitioners to easily explore different design choices and architectures, and leading to improved performance and reproducibility in various applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Condition on Empirical Noise in Diffusion-based Inverse Problems
PROPOSAL: Develop a new variant of diffusion models where the forward process is conditioned on empirical noise observations y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where η is the actual noise contaminating the measurements, rather than a fixed, analytical noise distribution. Call this reversed diffusion model the "Noise-conditioned Diffusion" (NCD).
CONTROLS: Comparison to analytical noise conditioning (e.g., current DDS and DDS-Var methods), MAP solver and Bayesian sampler baselines.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The NCD will be able to better capture the empirical noise structures, hence facilitating accurate reconstruction while also allowing better exploration of the solution space; it is likely to outperform current solvers in terms of reconstruction quality and robustness, especially in problems where the true noise is unknown. However, its performance may degrade on problems where the noise is Gaussian and known, as the analytical conditioning may be more accurate in such settings. 

We will add a second experiment and theoretically anchor this advance by proving the NCD method faces at most n/2 local minima in reasonal diffusion process depths, hence being able to find the global optimum even if initialized at random.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling from the Posterior with Manifold-Constrained Reversed Diffusion
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel sampler that leverages the Noise-conditioned Diffusion (NCD) from Proposal 1 and adds an additional constraint to enforce manifold feasibility during the reversed diffusion process. Specifically, introduce a probabilistic projection mechanism that ensures the intermediate states remain within a neighborhood of the data manifold learned during the NCD's forward process. This ensures that the denoiser is consistently fed on-manifold states, preserving the model's noise conditioning and preventing the artifacts that arise from off-manifold corrections.
CONTROLS: Same controls as Proposal 1, plus a comparison to the original NCD without manifold constraint.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This sampler will significantly improve over the NCD in terms of reconstruction quality, robustness, and interpretability by enforcing manifold feasibility, thus reducing the likelihood of off-manifold corrections and artifacts. It will also offer better exploration of the solution space, allowing for more accurate and diverse reconstructions. However, its performance may degrade on extremely ill-posed problems where the data manifold is highly degenerate and the manifold constraint might overly restrict the sampling process.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Leveraging Vae Lorentz Alignments for Improved Sampling
PROPOSAL (Revised 2): Introduce a novel manifold-constrained reversed diffusion approach that incorporates a VAE-aligned latent space for better alignment with the data manifold. Train a VAE on the preprocessed data, where pre-processing involves running a lower-depth version of the NCD to set a preliminary, high-resolution guess. This VAE can capture global structure and general patterns while nuisance factors are suppressed and selective learning happens. Then, leverage the aligned latent space to inform the manifold-constrained projection in the sampling process of the previous proposal. This enables more effective sampling of high-probability regions around the data manifold and fosters robust reconstructions despite complex noise statistics.
CONTROLS: Same controls as Proposal 2, plus an ablation study on the importance of the VAE-aligned latent space.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The VAE-alignment will significantly improve upon the previous method by enabling better detection of high-probability regions on the manifold, mitigating overfitting to off-manifold local minima and neglected by previous methodologies, leading to notably more robust, plausible reconstructions, more robustness to severe ill-posedness and better algorithmic convergence

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geometry of Measurement Noise: Towards Analyzing Diffusion-based Inverse Problem Solvers
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to analyze the geometry of measurement noise in diffusion-based inverse problems, providing insights into the topological properties of the input space and how it affects the solvers' performance. This includes a proof that the NCD method faces at most n/2 local minima in reasonable diffusion process depths, as claimed earlier, and further uses the probabilistic tools of stochastic differential equations and the theory of continuous-time Markov chains to derive requirements for the noise structure on the manifold, in order to ensure the convergence to the correct reconstruction solution. By providing a deeper understanding of the measurement noise's impact, this work aims to shed light on the solvers' behavior and identify areas for further improvement.
CONTROLS: Empirical evaluation on simple synthetic problems using the NCD and other diffusion-based solvers.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework will demonstrate that the NCD method's robustness to measurement noise can be rigorously justified by its geometry, providing an optimal upper bound on the number of local minima, that roughly matches the reported behavior. This contribution will be particularly insightful in poorly understood regimes.

PROPOSAL: Integrate a probabilistic uncertainty-aware framework into the manifold-constrained reversed diffusion sampling approach (Proposal 2). By leveraging the NCD's noise-conditioning properties and the manifold-constrained projection mechanism, introduce a probabilistic mechanism to quantify the uncertainty associated with the sampling process. Use this framework to adaptively adjust the sampling rates and guide the exploration of the solution space. This will enable the sampler to refine its reconstructions by iteratively refining the uncertainty estimates and updating the sampling process accordingly.
CONTROLS: Same controls as Proposal 2, plus an evaluation of the uncertainty-aware sampler using metrics such as expected calibration error (ECE) and predictive entropy.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The uncertainty-aware sampling framework will enhance the manifold-constrained reversed diffusion method by providing a principled way to quantify and mitigate its uncertainty, enabling the sampler to produce more accurate and plausible reconstructions while effectively handling cases with high or unknown measurement noise. However, its computational overhead may increase in comparison to the baseline, particularly for high-noise problems, that may necessitate the iteration with refinement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Robustness Enhancement via Adversarial Denoising
PROPOSAL: Develop a task-agnostic framework to enhance the robustness of diffusion-based inverse problem solvers to measurement noise, using adversarial denoising techniques. Train an adversarial denoiser (AD) to produce perturbed observations that are most beneficial for the solver's training, thus augmenting the solver's capacity to handle real-world noise. Integrate the AD into the learning pipeline to provide the solver with robustness promotion, augmenting its performance on diverse noise scenarios. This approach preserves the benefits of the current methodology and strengthen their resilience to real-world measurement uncertainties.
CONTROLS: Evaluate robustness against various noises (Gaussian, Poisson, impulsive) using metrics such as average mean squared error (MSE).
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The task-agnostic robustness enhancement framework will provide diffusion-based inverse problem solvers with increased resilience against diverse measurement noise types. This advancement will push current diffusion-based methodologies closest to invulnerability to noise, allowing users to tackle problems with complete fidelity, heralding the realization of ideal solutions in a noisy real world, while increasing robustness failure occurs not over intolerable noise levels, where other algorithms significantly perform badly as well.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dimension-wise Distribution Rectification for Distributionally Robust Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We investigate dimension-wise distribution rectification (DWR), a novel approach that adapts the dimension-wise distribution mismatch between the source and target domains by learning a domain-invariant transformation of the input features. Specifically, we propose to learn the optimal subset of features that should be transformed and the set of transformations for regularization. Our approach casts the problem as a bilevel optimization problem to learn the transformations and weighs the contribution of the labeled source data and unlabeled target data via an MDL-based objective. We will test DWR on classification benchmarks like CIFAR-10-C, CelebA-HQ and CUB.
CONTROLS: Baseline methods: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) on source data and standard domain adaptation baselines.
COST: ~100k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect DWR to show competitive performance with the state-of-the-art methods particularly when the source domain has significant spurious features and the number of unlabeled data in the target domain is limited. It might fail when the misalignment between source and target domains are mainly caused by the marginal distribution rather than conditional distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Loss Normalization for Robust Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: This proposal involves learning a domain-agnostic loss function that captures the discrepancy between the source and target distributions, which can be used to normalize the loss function during unsupervised domain adaptation. We explore a novel adversarial training scheme to learn the domain-agnostic loss function without target labels. Specifically, we design a meta-network that normalizes the source and target loss functions using an auxiliary classification network, and train the meta-network using an adversarial loss function to minimize the normalized loss. We aim to evaluate its performance on image classification benchmarks from the UDA literature such as Office-31, DomainNet, and append our results to DWR's baselines.
CONTROLS: Baseline methods: ERM on source data, standard UDA algorithms including DWR.
COST: ~50k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The main goal is to assess the benefits of the domain-agnostic approach, though it might also provide novel insight to DWR about its performances under adaptation tasks with under uniform loss criteria. It could fail if its normalized loss measures are consistently ill-defined or misleading, mainly by unstable meta-networks that overfit the overall meaningful large image predicates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain Invariant Graph Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: This proposal is a graph-based extension of DWR that can capture complex dependencies between features. We formulate the adaptation problem as a graph neural network (GNN) that learns a domain-invariant representation by folding in both the source and target samples. We propose to learn a graph that is invariant across domains and uses spectral methods to learn the graph Laplacian such that the basis obtained is domain-invariant. The key insight is that the domain-invariant graph captures the common structure and the relationships between features, making it a suitable representation for adaptation. We will also experiment it on instance based frameworks like VAEs and SCAs.
CONTROLS: Baseline methods: Standard GNNs on source data and DWR.
COST: ~80k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The inclusion of graph learning into DWR should capture non-linear relationships between the features more effectively and lessen the issue of failures caused by using some strong assumptions about structured distribution shifts between domains. However, it might increase the computational complexity and memory footprint of the method which might become a limitation for extremely large-scale settings.

TITLE: Graph-Based PDE Solver with Dynamic Option Type
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel graph-based neural PDE solver that incorporates a dynamic option type to capture the operator structure of the problem, which accounts for variations in the source terms across space and time. The solver is designed to learn a graph neural network (GNN) that represents the spatial dynamics, which takes as input a dynamic option type containing information about the source term. This approach can lead to a significant reduction in the learning space and exploration burden of the neural solver, enabling it to learn accurate spatiotemporal dynamics from a limited number of training trajectories.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the recent Graph-AC model, which is a state-of-the-art graph-based PDE solver that uses a fixed option type. We also vary the capacity of our dynamic option type (e.g., by reducing its dimensionality) as an ablation study.

PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform Graph-AC in terms of learning accuracy, especially in the presence of source terms with varying spatial and temporal patterns. However, we also predict that the dynamic option type may lead to overfitting if not properly regularized.

PROPOSAL: Train a conditional image generative model using a multi-task learning approach, where the model is trained to minimize two loss functions simultaneously: one for quality (e.g., pixel-wise reconstruction loss) and another for diversity (e.g., similarity between generated images and the real exemplars).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the multi-task learning model with the exemplar-based approach (proposal 1) and a standard conditional generative model.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours (1.5 days on 100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the multi-task learning model to improve both quality and diversity, as it learns to balance these competing objectives. However, the benefit may come at the cost of increased training time and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Directional Discriminative Loss for Exemplar-Grounded Diversity
PROPOSAL: Introduce a directional discriminative loss term to the exemplar-based approach (proposal 1), where the model is encouraged to generate images that are not only diverse from the real exemplars but also in a specific direction (e.g., more urban or more natural) as represented by the context.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the directional discriminative loss with the standard exemplar-based approach and the multi-task learning model (proposal 2).
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours (1.2 days on 100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the directional discriminative loss to improve the geographic diversity of generated images, particularly in the specific direction of interest. However, it may struggle with more complex relationships between context and generated images.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised loss with the standard exemplar-based approach, the multi-task learning model (proposal 2), and the original directional discriminative loss (proposal 3).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Heterogeneous Retriever Combining Techniques for Multimodal Visual Document Retrieval
PROPOSAL: We conduct an extensive ablation study, exploring different combining techniques for the hybrid retrieval of visual document retrieval, specifically focusing on lightweight dense text retrievers and ColPali-based encoders. Using the widely adopted MSMARCO dataset and matches collection and the retrieval setup from the ColBERT paper, we experiment with aggregation methods at the query-document similarity scores and document ranks, and evaluate the impact of various normalization techniques on the overall performance.
CONTROLS: We compare against the ColPali baseline and other state-of-the-art retrievers such as Ligero and HybridColBERT, both in stage 1 (document collection) and stage 2 (top-50 candidate ranking – normalized DCG metric). Additionally, we investigate the impact of embedding dimensionality and pooling method on the retrieval performance of the dense text retriever.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a moderate improvement ( around 10-15% mAP on the MS MARCO v2 test set) compared to the baseline, with the best result arising from an aggregation at document ranks combined with a learned normalization method for light dense retriever's embeddings. The contribution of the dense retriever might be higher for longer documents or those with rich layout structure, where captions or metadata are hard to extract.

TITLE: Efficient Gradient-Free Exploration in Continuous Action Spaces
PROPOSAL: Develop an actor-free, value-based algorithm that utilizes a Gaussian Process Q-Function to perform gradient-free exploration in continuous action spaces. At each step, sample actions from a Gaussian Process distribution centered around the most promising previously sampled action, with the Q-value of each sampled action used as a likelihood-like function to update the GP distribution. The uncertainty and variance of the Q-function updates will guide exploration to less likely regions, efficiently maximizing the expected improvement for the next sample. Use the efficient needle-in-haystack approximation to compute expectations with Gaussian Processes in a single forward pass.
CONTROLS: Q-learning with greedy action selection as baseline, additional experiments ablating the Gaussian Process Q-Function or removing the uncertainty-based exploration heuristic.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm achieves competitive or better performance compared to established actor-critic methods on various synthetic control tasks, while being more robust towards non-stationarity and variations in the Q-function landscape. However, it might struggle with very high-dimensional action spaces or when the GP model is poorly chosen.

TITLE: Bayesian Optimization with Stratified Sampling for Q-Function Maximization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a stratified sampling Bayesian optimization approach for efficient Q-function maximization within the actor-free framework. Divide the action space into stratified bins that optimize a posterior distribution of the Q-function's maximum, allocated based on previously evaluated Q-values and the global maximum's uncertainty. This allocation prioritizes promising regions while controlling the sampling distribution according to the available information. Use a Boyd-Balakrishnan global optimization algorithm to determine the strata boundaries, trading off between exploration and the accuracy of the Q-function's maximum.

PREDICTION: This stratified sampling approach has the potential to outperform existing actor-free methods in high-dimensional or hard to optimize action spaces due to the more efficient allocation of evaluations. Considerations remain for algorithms that diverge or get stuck within strata during optimization.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method that combines label smoothing with smoothed argmax to enable end-to-end, gradient-based training of one-step discrete generators distilled from Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs). PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in the performance of the one-step generator with our proposed method, outperforming the baseline and state-of-the-art methods. The method may fail in cases where the label smoothing factor is too high, leading to unstable training.

TITLE: Dynamic Step Control for Bandwidth-Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Implement a step-size control mechanism that adaptively terminates the diffusion process based on a proxy for available bandwidth. This could be done by monitoring the model's output quality and compressed file size at each step and adjusting the step size accordingly to meet the target bitrate. The step size control can be learned jointly with the diffusion model through reinforcement learning.

ACTION: REVISE 1

This will allow the model to not only adapt the number of steps based on available bandwidth, but also to focus on regions that are most important for image quality at the given bitrate.

TITLE: Graph Structure Transformer for Robust OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel graph structure transformer, GST, that can selectively filter out structural redundancy in test graphs at test time, without modifying the pre-trained GNN. GST introduces an attention mechanism that identifies essential nodes in the test graph and discards redundant nodes by learning a graph attention mask that attenuates the contribution of redundant nodes. This enables the pre-trained GNN to focus on distinctive structural information and improve OOD detection.

COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GST is expected to outperform GOODAT and the baseline, achieving higher AUROC and AUPRC on real-world benchmarks, particularly in molecular property prediction and drug discovery.

Inspired by the recent success of transformer-based models in hierarchical frequency decompositions [5], we will propose a novel frequency-aware tokenizer that dynamically adjusts the attention weights of the transformer layers to capture frequency-dependent relationships in PDE solution manifolds. This frequency-aware transformer architecture will be tested on various FNO models and PDE tasks, including shallow-water simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics.
CONTROLS: The performance of our proposed frequency-aware transformer architecture will be compared with existing models, such as learned soft prompts, SLoRA, and full-model fine-tuning, on the specified PDE tasks.
COST: Estimated 40 GPU-hours (two A100 GPUs for 20 hours each, with mixed precision).
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the frequency-aware transformer architecture will leverage the hierarchical frequency structure of PDE solutions, offering improved fine-tuning performance on complex tasks such as shallow-water simulation and solar magnetohydrodynamics.

TITLE: Drafting Velocity in Flow Matching for Reduced Inference Latency
PROPOSAL: Design a draft model for FM by minimizing the KL divergence between the full model's velocity field and the draft's velocity field at the current step, using a small set of parallelized samples. Train the draft model on synthetic data generated with low-resolution FM models, and evaluate its ability to create high-resolution samples that are consistent with the full model's output.
CONTROLS: Compare with a control model where the draft model's velocity predictions are randomly initialized, and ablate the KL divergence objective function to see its necessary contribution to the task.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (training the draft model on synthetic data)
PREDICTION: Expected result: latency is reduced by 30% without significant loss in output quality, where the failure is that the draft model may resort to local optima, as the KL divergence is used as an approximation rather than an exact match of the full model's velocity predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Draft Velocities in Flow Matching
PROPOSAL: Propose two methods to evaluate draft velocities in FM, determine whether a draft's trajectory deviates from the full model's trajectory. The first is drift-aware online ablation: insert iterative displacements between each full step and its corresponding draft step, and estimate drift through optimal transport distance between the interpolated velocities of the two. The second is an image discrimination task (IDS) on the differences between the draft and full steps, conditioned on the draft's current location in the trajectory. Evaluate these methods on a set of real-world images generated by a pre-trained FM model, in terms of how accurately they detect divergence from the full model's output.
CONTROLS: Compare with random feature selection and with self-supervised evaluation methods, such as auto-encoding (AE).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (image generation and analysis)
PREDICTION: Expected result: the IDS method is more effective than the drift-aware online ablation method in capturing the accuracy of the draft velocities, where the failure modes include failure to generalize across a wider range of models and lack of interpretability for users.

TITLE: Large Language Model-based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Go
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach of combining a pre-trained large language model with deep reinforcement learning to master the game of Go. Specifically, we will use a state-of-the-art LLM as the agent's policy network, which will generate a move based on the current board position and the agent's knowledge base. The agent will receive a reward signal based on the game outcome, and the policy will be updated using proximal policy optimization algorithm. We will train the agent on a combination of Go games against itself and human players.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the AlphaGo paper (silver, 2016), and ablate our model by removing the LLM policy network and using a random agent for comparison.
COST: 50,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach will significantly outperform the random agent, and might even surpass some of the human players', but it may struggle to reach the level of AlphaGo. The performance will likely degrade rapidly during the training process, but with careful data augmentation and pruning strategy, we can optimise the performance for a range of gameplay variations.
